What this means for investors

Up-and-coming neocloud Nebius announced a $4.5 billion convertible note offering today, with $2.75 billion due in 2030, $1.75 billion due in 2034, and an option to buy $675 million in additional notes. Nebius shares sank 10% today on the news, as the major transaction will likely be dilutive to shareholders over the short term, but will provide the company with valuable cash to build out its AI infrastructure.

title: IBM Stock Is Out Of Favor, But The Margin Commitment Never Came Down
detail:
IBM Stock Is Out Of Favor, But The Margin Commitment Never Came Down
Trefis Team
Wed, August 19, 2026 at 1:01 PM PDT 3 min read
IBM
ACN
ORCL-PD
GOOG
AMZN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by StockSnap on Pixabay

The revenue guidance came down after the second-quarter miss; the operating pretax margin and free-cash-flow commitments did not.

International Business Machines (IBM) has traded essentially flat over the past year while the S&P 500 returned about 20%, and the shares now sit near 71% of their 52-week high. The company also cut its 2026 revenue growth guide after a fiscal Q2 2026 shortfall. The number worth arguing about is not the revenue line that slipped, but the profit commitment management did not move with it.

The Revenue Guide Came Down, And The 100-Basis-Point Margin Guide Did Not

The new revenue growth range is 4% to 5%, down from the 5%-plus management was defending in April. The company still expects 100 basis points of operating pretax margin expansion in 2026, matching the roughly one point it guided to in April, and still expects free cash flow to grow by about $1 billion, with productivity actions more than offsetting the revenue-related headwinds. Set against $69.1 billion of trailing-twelve-month revenue, that unchanged profit commitment is the more informative half of the guidance: the shortfall moved the sales line and management re-underwrote the profit line anyway.

From 14.4% To 18.4%, A Margin That Has Not Stopped Climbing

Operating pretax margin climbed steadily from 14.4% in 2023 to 15.5% in 2024, reached 17.1% in 2025, and now sits at 18.4% over the trailing twelve months. A pretax profit line that keeps widening while the top line disappoints is the part of the bull case with three years of history behind it. Margins that hold their direction like that are one of the properties the Trefis High Quality Portfolio favors in its holdings. Management describes its productivity program in operational terms: AI and automation deployed at greater scale across the company, third-party spend reduced, and AI used to make software development more efficient. In fiscal Q2 2026, that program landed unevenly, with Consulting segment profit margin up 160 basis points and Software up 110 basis points on those actions while Infrastructure fell 150 basis points on IBM Z mainframe mix.

Deferred or Destroyed Is Still the Question Margin Cannot Answer

None of this answers whether the demand is deferred or destroyed, and the margin case does not pretend to. Management says the software shortfall was limited to a capital-expenditure-sensitive corner of the portfolio: transaction processing revenue fell 9% while data grew 18%, after clients redirected spending toward servers, storage and memory ahead of expected price increases. That software is bought inside the enterprise license agreements clients sign alongside mainframes, so a budget shift away from mainframe deals and toward that other hardware pulls the software with it. About a third of the slipped deals closed in the first three weeks of fiscal Q3 2026, which management calls an indication rather than full evidence. The miss did cost something: operating gross profit margin fell 70 basis points in fiscal Q2 2026, largely on the revenue shortfall and mix. Productivity actions ran ahead of plan in the same quarter, and the operating pretax margin still expanded 30 basis points. So the case is not that margin cancels that question, but that the profit line widened through the quarter that raised it, which is worth weighing against how other beaten-down names have behaved after falls of this size.

title: Nvidia credit risk gauge hits new peak as SoftBank readies record bond issue
detail:
Nvidia credit risk gauge hits new peak as SoftBank readies record bond issue
Senad Karaahmetovic
Wed, August 19, 2026 at 2:56 AM PDT 3 min read
9984.T
NVDA
ORCL-PD
9984
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investing.com - SoftBank Group is preparing to issue approximately 1 trillion yen ($6.26 billion) in seven-year corporate bonds targeting Japanese retail investors, a sale that would be the largest of its kind ever by a Japanese company.

The offering lands at a fraught moment for AI-linked credit globally, with Nvidia's 5-year credit default swap spread surpassing its late-July peak and long-term government yields reaching their highest levels in decades.

SoftBank is the most visible Asian proxy for the AI financing wave, having already raised a 1.6 billion yen hybrid bond in May 2026. The scale of the planned retail deal — set against record-high sovereign yields — makes it a direct test of whether retail demand in Japan can absorb AI infrastructure debt as institutional credit markets grow more selective.

Long-term borrowing costs from the U.S. to Germany and Japan hit their highest levels in decades, with investors pointing squarely at hyperscaler bond supply as a contributing force.

AI infrastructure debt now accounts for as much as 30% of net new issuance in some investment-grade indexes this year, according to private credit market commentary cited by Reuters.

Longer-duration corporate yields moved above 6% in July, raising all-in income from high-quality corporate credit but also driving greater investor selectivity given elevated issuance and tight starting valuations.

Japan's broader retail-targeted corporate bond market is on pace to hit a record 2.8 trillion yen this year, per Nikkei, suggesting demand has not dried up, but SoftBank's offering would dwarf anything attempted before.

Nvidia illustrates the credit stress building across the AI complex. Its 5-year CDS bid spread climbed to 80.77 basis points as of August 19, surpassing its late-July peak. That spread has risen roughly 90% year-to-date and more than doubled since late May.

Some of the widening reflects the simple mechanics of a larger debt stock to hedge rather than an imminent default scenario and Alphabet's recent bond sale in Australia still drew strong investor demand.

However, the directional signal is hard to ignore ahead of Nvidia's earnings report scheduled for next Wednesday, the first major test of its $500 billion AI financing narrative under capital-market scrutiny.

Nvidia has said it may back no more than 25% of the total itself, meaning the bulk of that capital must be raised externally into a market where yield competition from sovereigns is intensifying.

Oracle offers the starkest credit warning in the sector. Its 5-year CDS spread surpassed 200 basis points in July 2026, approximately four times the investment-grade corporate index and a level not seen since the 2008 financial crisis.

Chicago, IL – August 19, 2026 – Zacks.com announces the list of stocks featured in the Analyst Blog. Every day the Zacks Equity Research analysts discuss the latest news and events impacting stocks and the financial markets. Stocks recently featured in the blog include: Oracle Corp. ORCL, Microsoft MSFT, Amazon AMZN and Alphabet GOOGL.

Here are highlights from Tuesday's Analyst Blog:

Should You Buy Oracle Stock Despite Its Big AI Datacenter Bet?

Oracle Corp. has turned itself into one of the most talked-about names in enterprise technology, largely because of the scale of its bet on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure. The company is spending tens of billions of dollars building out AI data centers, funded partly through debt and equity issuance, and that capital intensity has made some investors nervous about the near-term path of free cash flow.

Yet a closer look at Oracle's underlying business, its rapidly expanding AI partnerships and its own forward-looking guidance suggests the near-term setup still favors buyers who can stomach the balance-sheet risk tied to this build-out, rather than investors waiting for full clarity before committing capital.

Shares of Oracle have lost 8.9% in the past six-month period, underperforming the Zacks Computer and Technology sector's appreciation of 21.7%, a gap that reflects investor caution around Oracle's debt-funded capital spending rather than any slowdown in its underlying AI business.

AI-Driven Cloud Backlog Underpins the Growth Case

The clearest fundamental signal comes from Oracle's Remaining Performance Obligations, which reached $638 billion at the end of the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, up 363% year over year and $85 billion sequentially. Most of that increase reflects large-scale AI contracts, and importantly, the prepaid and customer-supplied hardware portions of these agreements now total $75 billion, which meaningfully reduces the amount of capital Oracle itself must raise to build its AI data centers going forward. 

Cloud infrastructure revenues surged 93% in the quarter to $5.8 billion, while the Oracle Multicloud AI Database grew 404%, making it the company's fastest-growing business ever. These figures point to underlying demand that is outrunning Oracle's aggressive capacity additions, a dynamic that should keep utilization and eventually margins moving in the right direction as newly built megawatts of data center capacity come online through fiscal 2027.
